Where it began

Shikhar Dhawan was born in Delhi on 5 December 1985 and went to St. Mark's school in Meera Bagh. From the age of 12 he trained at the Sonnet Club under the coach Tarak Sinha, and he arrived there as a wicketkeeper. He is right-handed and writes that way, yet he learned to bat the other way round, which turned out to be a fine idea.

The runs came early. At the Under-19 World Cup of 2004, played in Bangladesh, nobody made more than his 505 runs, three hundreds among them, and he was named Player of the Tournament. Later that year he made his first-class debut for Delhi, and in 2007–08 he helped them win the Ranji Trophy.

The player

He waited a long time for his Test chance, and when it came, at Mohali against Australia in March 2013, he took it at a gallop. Handed his cap by Sachin Tendulkar, he reached three figures in 85 balls, the fastest hundred anyone had made on Test debut, and went on to 187 from 174 balls, the highest debut score by an Indian.

In 34 Tests between 2013 and 2018 he made 2,315 runs at 40.61, with seven hundreds. His best was 190 against Sri Lanka at Galle in 2017, on a tour where India won all three Tests and he was player of the series. In June 2018, against Afghanistan, he reached a hundred before lunch on the first morning of a Test, something no Indian had done before.

What made him special

Put him in a big tournament and he came alive. When India won the 2013 Champions Trophy he made more runs than anyone and was named its best player, topped the scoring again at the 2017 Champions Trophy, and was India's highest scorer at the 2015 World Cup. He was the first man to win the Champions Trophy's golden bat twice. In World Cups and Champions Trophies together he averaged 65.15, higher than anyone else who made 1,000 runs in them.

Test cricket was a moodier friend. He had spells when the runs dried up, and England in 2014 was one of them, but more than once he found his way back with a big hundred.

Away from the middle

Wisden named him one of its Cricketers of the Year in 2014, and in 2021 the Government of India gave him the Arjuna Award. In the Indian Premier League he became the first batter to make hundreds in consecutive matches, in 2020, and two years later only Virat Kohli had passed 6,000 runs in the competition before him. He announced his retirement from all cricket on 24 August 2024, and later that year turned out for Karnali Yaks in the Nepal Premier League.

And finally

His first one-day international, against Australia at Visakhapatnam in 2010, lasted two balls. The second bowled him. Few careers have started so quietly and ended with so many runs on the biggest stages.
